name: Newgrange
about: Newgrange (Sí an Bhrú), Brú na Bóinne, Co. Meath: a Neolithic passage tomb of c. 3200 BC - a cairn of water-rolled pebbles about 85 m across and 11 m high retained by 97 kerbstones, with a 19 m passage (22 + 21 orthostats) rising about 2 m to a cruciform chamber with a 6 m corbelled vault, three recesses and four basins, and a roof-box above the entrance that admits the winter solstice sunrise. Twelve stones of a Great Circle survive round it. The vault is original; the passage orthostats were straightened and the passage roof and roof-box dismantled and rebuilt in 1963-; the quartz-and-granite facade (to about 3 m), the kerb exposure, the curved entrance walls (modern, for visitors), a concrete wall behind the facade and a cowl over the chamber date from M. J. O'Kelly's excavation and reconstruction (1962-75) and later repairs (1984-88). Research file for a 3D model; quotes are exact text from the cited pages.

alignment.claim: Sunlight enters through the roof-box slit (not the doorway), runs up the passage and lights the chamber floor. O'Kelly, 21 December 1967: sun's upper edge at 8.54 GMT, beam in at 8.58, a 17 cm band, narrowing at 9.09, cut off at 9.15: 17 minutes.

cites.quote: At exactly 8.54 hours GMT the top edge of the ball of the sun appeared above the local horizon and at 8.58 hours, the first pencil of direct sunlight shone through the roofbox
As the thin line of light widened to a 17 cm-band and swung across the chamber floor
at exactly 9.15 hours, the direct beam was cut off from the tomb
For 17 minutes, therefore, at sunrise on the shortest day of the year
Michael J. O'Kelly was the first person in modern times to observe this event on 21 December 1967.

debate.claim: How far quartz was used round the mound: C. O'Kelly says 'at least in the entrance area'; Wikipedia says the facade covers part of the circumference.

cites.quote: White quartz stones were used as an outside finishing layer, at least in the entrance area.
covering part of the circumference

debate.claim: Roof-box authenticity: a 2016 claim that it was fabricated was refuted; it is photographed from the early 1900s. Hensey asks whether reports of the solstice influenced its reconstruction.

cites.quote: it has been recorded photographically since the early 1900s
to what extent may pre-excavation reports of a winter solstice connection with Newgrange have influenced the reconstruction

debate.claim: Date and completeness of the Great Circle: Bronze Age addition, or Neolithic (Williams 2023); whether the ring was ever complete is open.

whether a full ring was erected remains uncertain

gaps: No quoted single azimuth for the passage axis; only Ray's (133°49'-137°29') and Patrick's light windows and Coffey's c. 132°. Prendergast's total-station survey value is in the 2024 report's figures (Figure 3 shows 134-137°) and in Prendergast's papers (e.g. 'Facing the Sun', Archaeology Ireland 2017), not reachable as text.
Where and how much the passage bends: only 'sinuous' (Ray). O'Kelly 1982 (pp. 21-35, fig. of passage plan) has the orthostat-by-orthostat plan; no free text found.
Passage width along its length (only 'about 1 m'; Wakeman 1903 for the entrance) and the floor profile are in O'Kelly 1982 and the 2024 report's Figure 4 plan.

Per-stone sizes of kerbstones other than K1, of the 43 passage orthostats, and of the Great Circle stones (only the four tallest 2-2.5 m); GC positions are on O'Kelly's plan (copyright). Only 5 GC stones are on OSM.
Size of the closing (door) stone: only a popular '5-ton slab'; O'Kelly 1982 p. 35 describes it.
Facade length round the circumference and its exact plan; Hensey and Shee Twohig 2017 'Facing the cairn at Newgrange' (cited by Wikipedia) was not found online.

UNESCO whc.unesco.org and mythicalireland.com refused the checker; knowth.com and newgrange.com are secondary (Anthony Murphy) and decode with mojibake, so quotes from them avoid non-ASCII characters (except Ray's text, see source note).

No free-licence plan of the passage and chamber was found on Commons; the public-domain Coffey (1890s) and Wilde (1849) plans would need checking page by page and show the pre-restoration tilted orthostats.
